claim: Male C57BL/6J mice were given 6 weeks of intermittent access to alcohol (EtOH), a protocol known to induce heavy voluntary drinking.
source: Male C57BL/6J mice were given 6 weeks of intermittent access to alcohol (EtOH), a protocol known to induce heavy voluntary drinking (Hwa et al., 2011), before behavioral testing during protracted (7–10 days) abstinence [Figure 1A].
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hwa et al., 2011 and references Figure 1A showing the experimental protocol.

claim: Mice consumed high amounts of EtOH and increased their EtOH preference over time.
source: Mice consumed high amounts of EtOH [Figure 1B] and increased their EtOH preference over time [Figure 1C].
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Mice achieved greater than 80 mg/dl blood EtOH concentrations, indicative of intoxication, which correlated with drinking behavior.
source: Further, mice achieved greater than 80 mg/dl blood EtOH concentrations, indicative of intoxication, which correlated with drinking behavior [Figure 1D; R2 = 0.59, p=0.0036].
evidence: The claim is supported by blood EtOH concentration data shown in Figure 1D with statistical correlation (R2 = 0.59, p=0.0036).

claim: Both water (H2O)-drinking controls and EtOH drinking mice showed a TMT-induced increase in plasma corticosterone.
source: Both water (H2O)-drinking controls and EtOH drinking mice showed a TMT-induced increase in plasma corticosterone [Figure 1E; TMT main effect: F1,10=26.79, p=0.0004, H2O BL vs TMT t10 = 3.32, p=0.0154, EtOH BL vs TMT t10 = 3.99, p=0.005].
evidence: The claim is supported by plasma corticosterone data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis showing significant TMT main effect.

claim: EtOH-drinking mice displayed reduced avoidance of the TMT compared to the water (H2O)-drinking controls during protracted abstinence.
source: EtOH-drinking mice displayed reduced avoidance of the TMT compared to the water (H2O)-drinking controls during protracted abstinence [Figure 1G–H].
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 1G-H.

claim: EtOH drinkers demonstrated reduced burying behavior compared to controls.
source: Specifically, EtOH drinkers demonstrated reduced burying behavior compared to controls [Figure 1I].
evidence: The claim is supported by burying behavior data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Systemic treatment with 5 mg/kg of the long-acting KOR antagonist norBNI 16 hr prior to TMT exposure reduced EtOH-induced increases in TMT contact compared to saline-injected EtOH mice.
source: Systemic treatment with 5 mg/kg of the long-acting KOR antagonist norBNI 16 hr prior to TMT exposure reduced EtOH-induced increases in TMT contact compared to saline-injected EtOH mice [Figure 1G; Drug main effect F1,35=5.45, p=0.0254, EtOH main effect F1,35=15.80, p=0.0003; saline H2O vs EtOH t35 = 2.95, p=0.0113; EtOH saline vs norBNI t35 = 4.12, p=0.0004].
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis showing significant drug and EtOH main effects.

claim: NorBNI alleviated reductions in burying behavior in EtOH mice compared to saline-injected EtOH drinkers.
source: NorBNI also alleviated reductions in burying behavior in EtOH mice compared to saline-injected EtOH drinkers [Figure 1I; interaction F1,35=9.70, p=0.0037; saline H2O vs saline EtOH t35 = 4.52, p=0.0001; EtOH saline vs norBNI t35 = 2.47, p=0.0367].
evidence: The claim is supported by burying behavior data shown in Figure 1I with statistical analysis showing significant interaction effect.

claim: EtOH mice showed reduced time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze.
source: EtOH mice showed reduced time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze [Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; t18 = 2.81, p=0.0115] and equal time in the closed arms as controls [Figure 1—figure supplement 2C].
evidence: The claim is supported by elevated plus maze data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B with statistical analysis.

claim: TMT elicited robust dorsal BNST c-Fos immunostaining, which was greater in EtOH mice compared to H2O mice.
source: TMT elicited robust dorsal BNST c-Fos immunostaining, which was greater in EtOH mice compared to H2O mice [Figure 2B–C; interaction F1,23=12.45, p=0.0018; H2O non-stress (NS) vs TMT t23 = 6.51, p<0.0001; EtOH NS vs TMT t23 = 10.13, p<0.0001; TMT H2O vs TMT EtOH t23 = 3.92, p=0.0041].
evidence: The claim is supported by c-Fos immunostaining data shown in Figures 2B-C with statistical analysis showing significant interaction effect.

claim: TMT increased expression of Pdyn GFP-expressing neurons in the BNST versus non-stressed (NS) mice.
source: Furthermore, TMT increased expression of Pdyn GFP-expressing neurons in the BNST versus non-stressed (NS) mice [Figure 2D; TMT main effect F1,23=4.56, p=0.0437].
evidence: The claim is supported by Pdyn-GFP expression data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis showing significant TMT main effect.

claim: Colocalization of c-Fos in Pdyn-containing cells (BNSTPDYN) was largest in the stressed EtOH group.
source: Importantly, colocalization of c-Fos in Pdyn-containing cells (BNSTPDYN) was largest in the stressed EtOH group [Figure 2E; interaction F1,23=5.91, p=0.0233; EtOH NS vs TMT t23 = 4.66, p=0.0007; TMT H2O vs TMT EtOH t23 = 3.65, p=0.0081], suggesting an interaction between EtOH, Pdyn, and predator odor stress in the BNST.
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis showing significant interaction effect.

claim: Pdyn expression was heightened in the EtOH group compared to H2O group.
source: Pdyn expression was heightened in the EtOH group compared to H2O group [Fig G-H, Pdyn intensity: t10 = 2.99, p=0.0136; Figure 2I, Pdyn counts: t10 = 2.21, p=0.0512], but Oprk1 expression was not altered [Figure 2J].
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 2G-I with statistical analysis showing significant difference in Pdyn intensity.

claim: Intra-BNST norBNI reduced contact with TMT in the EtOH mice.
source: However, similar to systemic administration, intra-BNST norBNI reduced contact with TMT in the EtOH mice [Figure 3E; interaction F1,35=4.30, p=0.0454; PBS H2O vs EtOH t35 = 3.29, p=0.0105; EtOH PBS vs norBNI t35 = 3.32, p=0.0105] with no effect on time spent in the far corners of the home cage [Figure 3F].
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis showing significant interaction effect.

claim: EtOH mice showed significantly less burying behavior in response to TMT compared to H2O mice, but there was no effect of drug in EtOH mice.
source: EtOH mice showed significantly less burying behavior in response to TMT compared to H2O mice, but there was no effect of drug in EtOH mice [Figure 3G; EtOH main effect F1,35=42.65, p<0.001; PBS H2O vs EtOH t35 = 4.06, p=0.0010; norBNI H2O vs EtOH t35 = 5.19, p<0.001].
evidence: The claim is supported by burying behavior data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis showing significant EtOH main effect.

claim: TMT increased sEPSC frequency (Hz) in EtOH and H2O drinkers compared to non-stressed (NS) mice.
source: TMT increased sEPSC frequency (Hz) in EtOH and H2O drinkers compared to non-stressed (NS) mice [Figure 4B; TMT main effect F1,50=18.24, p<0.0001; H2O NS vs TMT t50 = 3.38, p=0.0028; EtOH NS vs TMT t50 = 2.75, p=0.0167] with no alterations in sIPSC frequency [Figure 4C].
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis showing significant TMT main effect.

claim: Increased sEPSC/sIPSC ratios reflected heightened excitatory drive onto BNSTPDYN cells in stressed mice regardless of drinking history.
source: Increased sEPSC/sIPSC ratios also reflected heightened excitatory drive onto BNSTPDYN cells in stressed mice regardless of drinking history [Figure 4D; TMT main effect F1,50=23.61, p<0.0001; H2O NS vs TMT t50 = 2.50, p=0.0312; EtOH NS vs TMT t50 = 4.24, p=0.0002; TMT H2O vs EtOH t50 = 2.25, p=0.0566].
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4D with statistical analysis showing significant TMT main effect.

claim: Systemic norBNI pretreatment reduced sEPSC frequency in BNSTPDYN cells.
source: Systemic norBNI pretreatment reduced sEPSC frequency in BNSTPDYN cells [Figure 4E–F; norBNI main effect F1,34=7.94, p=0.008, EtOH TMT saline vs norBNI t34 = 3.22, p=0.0056], but not sIPSC frequency [Figure 4G], with an increase in the sEPSC/sIPSC ratio being suppressed by norBNI in the EtOH TMT mice [Figure 4H; norBNI main effect F1,34=9.36, p=0.0043; EtOH TMT saline vs norBNI t34 = 2.62, p=0.026].
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 4E-H with statistical analysis showing significant norBNI main effects.

claim: Pdyn deletion in the BNST did not alter EtOH consumption.
source: Pdyn deletion in the BNST did not alter EtOH consumption [Figure 5C–D; Time main effect F17,323=3.28, p=0.0095; Cumulative EtOH drinking (g/kg) per group: t19 = 0.23, p=0.8181] or preference [Figure 5E–F; Time main effect F17,323=4.09, p=0.0019; average EtOH preference per group: t19 = 0.10, p=0.9221].
evidence: The claim is supported by drinking behavior data shown in Figures 5C-F with statistical analysis showing no significant group differences.

claim: EtOH mice with BNST Pdyn deletion suppressed EtOH-related increases in TMT contact.
source: EtOH mice with BNST Pdyn deletion suppressed EtOH-related increases in TMT contact [Figure 5G, Figure 5I; EtOH main effect F1,37=7.31, p=0.0103. GFP H2O vs EtOH t37 = 2.93, p=0.0347], and they increased their burying behavior compared to control EtOH mice [Figure 5K; interaction F1,37=4.51, p=0.0405. EtOH GFP vs EtOH Cre-GFP t37 = 3.91, p=0.0419].
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 5G, 5I, and 5K with statistical analysis showing significant effects.

claim: A large proportion of BNSTPDYN neurons were light responsive after TMT in both H2O and EtOH mice, whereas non-stressed H2O mice had mostly non-responsive cells.
source: A large proportion of BNSTPDYN neurons were light responsive after TMT in both H2O and EtOH mice, whereas non-stressed H2O mice had mostly non-responsive cells [Figure 6C; Χ23 = 21.43, p<0.0001].
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis using chi-square test.

claim: EtOH mice had larger monosynaptic optically-evoked EPSC (oEPSC) amplitudes following TMT compared to H2O mice and non-stressed EtOH mice.
source: Similarly, EtOH mice had larger monosynaptic optically-evoked EPSC (oEPSC) amplitudes following TMT compared to H2O mice and non-stressed EtOH mice [Figure 6D; interaction F1,33=4.74, p=0.0367; H2O non-stress (NS) vs EtOH + TMT t33 = 3.70, p=0.0047; EtOH NS vs EtOH + TMT t33 = 4.50, p=0.0005], with no effects on paired pulse ratio [Figure 6E].
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6D with statistical analysis showing significant interaction effect.

claim: Both AMPA and NMDA peak amplitudes were greater in BNSTPDYN EtOH TMT mice compared to unstressed EtOH mice and H2O mice.
source: Both AMPA and NMDA peak amplitudes were greater in BNSTPDYN EtOH TMT mice compared to unstressed EtOH mice and H2O mice [Figure 6F–G; AMPA peak amplitude: TMT main effect F1,34=22.03, p<0.0001; H2O NS vs EtOH + TMT t34 = 4.28, p=0.0009; EtOH NS vs EtOH + TMT t34 = 4.82, p=0.0002. NMDA peak amplitude: TMT main effect F1,34=12.09, p=0.0148; H2O NS vs EtOH + TMT t34 = 3.13, p=0.0213; EtOH NS vs EtOH + TMT t34 = 3.27, p=0.0148].
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data shown in Figures 6F-G with statistical analysis showing significant TMT main effects.

claim: There was an increase in the AMPA/NMDA ratio in the EtOH TMT mice.
source: There was also an increase in the AMPA/NMDA ratio in the EtOH TMT mice [Figure 6H; TMT main effect F1,34=8.12, p=0.0074; EtOH NS vs EtOH + TMT t34 = 2.89, p=0.0132], suggesting alcohol drinking may prime the synapse for AMPA receptor recruitment, further contributing to aberrant glutamate signaling and stress reactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6H with statistical analysis showing significant TMT main effect.

claim: The EtOH TMT mice were more resistant to synaptic depression of oEPSC amplitude in response to repeated 1 Hz oEPSC pulses, suggesting alterations in short-term plasticity.
source: In addition, the EtOH TMT mice were also more resistant to synaptic depression of oEPSC amplitude in response to repeated 1 Hz oEPSC pulses, suggesting alterations in short-term plasticity [Figure 6I–L; interaction F27,351=1.83, p=0.0080; Pulse 3: EtOH NS vs EtOH + TMT t22.81=3.21, p=0.0234; H2O + TMT vs EtOH + TMT t18.81=3.40, p=0.0180; Pulse 4: EtOH NS vs EtOH + TMT t23.99=3.95, p=0.0036].
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data shown in Figures 6I-L with statistical analysis showing significant interaction effect.

claim: EtOH drinking and TMT exposure did not affect BLA-BNST oEPSC amplitude.
source: In contrast to the mPFC-BNST pathway, EtOH drinking and TMT exposure did not affect BLA-BNST oEPSC amplitude [Figure 6—figure supplement 1C], paired pulse ratio [Figure 6—figure supplement 1D], AMPA peak amplitude [Figure 6—figure supplement 1E], NMDA peak amplitude [Figure 6—figure supplement 1F], or AMPA/NMDA ratio [Figure 6—figure supplement 1G].
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-G showing no significant effects.

claim: The inhibitory DREADD alone did not affect drinking behavior across the 6 weeks.
source: The inhibitory DREADD alone did not affect drinking behavior across the 6 weeks [Figure 7E] or short-term drinking behavior when CNO was injected versus saline [Figure 7F–H].
evidence: The claim is supported by drinking behavior data shown in Figures 7E-H showing no significant effects.

claim: hM4Di-mediated inhibition of the mPFC-BNST pathway reduced contact with TMT in both H2O and EtOH mice.
source: When exposed to TMT, hM4Di-mediated inhibition of the mPFC-BNST pathway did not alter distance traveled [Figure 7J], but it did reduce contact with TMT in both H2O and EtOH mice [Figure 7I, Figure 7K; virus main effect: F1,25=5.37, p=0.0289; no significant post-hoc differences].
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figures 7I, 7J, and 7K with statistical analysis showing significant virus main effect.

claim: mPFC-BNST inhibition increased burying behavior in EtOH-drinking mice.
source: mPFC-BNST inhibition also increased burying behavior in EtOH-drinking mice [Figure 7M; EtOH main effect: F1,25=13.80, p=0.001; virus main effect: F1,25=16.47, p=0.004; H2O mCherry vs EtOH mCherry t25 = 4.37, p=0.0234; EtOH mCherry vs EtOH hM4Di t25 = 4.72, p=0.0131].
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7M with statistical analysis showing significant EtOH and virus main effects.

claim: Exposure to predator odor during protracted withdrawal from intermittent alcohol drinking resulted in enhanced prefrontal cortex (PFC)-driven excitation of prodynorphin-containing neurons in the BNST.
source: Exposure to predator odor during protracted withdrawal from intermittent alcohol drinking resulted in enhanced prefrontal cortex (PFC)-driven excitation of prodynorphin-containing neurons in the BNST.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic electrophysiology data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of prodynorphin in the BNST restored abnormal responses to predator odor in alcohol-exposed mice.
source: Furthermore, deletion of prodynorphin in the BNST and chemogenetic inhibition of the PFC-BNST pathway restored abnormal responses to predator odor in alcohol-exposed mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data from genetic deletion and chemogenetic experiments.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of the PFC-BNST pathway restored abnormal responses to predator odor in alcohol-exposed mice.
source: Furthermore, deletion of prodynorphin in the BNST and chemogenetic inhibition of the PFC-BNST pathway restored abnormal responses to predator odor in alcohol-exposed mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data from chemogenetic experiments.

claim: Kappa opioid receptor signaling in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) is a critical molecular substrate underlying abnormal stress responses to predator odor following heavy alcohol drinking.
source: Here, we show that kappa opioid receptor signaling in the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) is a critical molecular substrate underlying abnormal stress responses to predator odor following heavy alcohol drinking.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological and genetic manipulation data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Prolonged alcohol drinking and withdrawal experiences result in enhanced responsiveness and behavioral sensitivity to stress during protracted abstinence.
source: Prolonged alcohol drinking and withdrawal experiences result in enhanced responsiveness and behavioral sensitivity to stress during protracted abstinence (Heilig et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Heilig et al., 2010.

claim: Clinical studies show that negative stress coping is predictive of higher levels of drinking in alcoholics.
source: Reciprocally, clinical studies show that negative stress coping is predictive of higher levels of drinking in alcoholics (Noone et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Noone et al., 1999.

claim: Blunted responses to stress have been identified in alcohol-dependent people.
source: As blunted responses to stress have been identified in alcohol-dependent people (Sinha et al., 2011), it is essential to consider mechanisms by which alcohol drinking impacts stress responses during protracted abstinence.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sinha et al., 2011.

claim: Chronic alcohol exposure engages brain stress signaling systems that influence drinking behaviors in a dynamic and complex manner.
source: Chronic alcohol exposure engages brain stress signaling systems that influence drinking behaviors in a dynamic and complex manner (Koob and Kreek, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koob and Kreek, 2007.

claim: The neuropeptide prodynorphin (Pdyn) and its receptor, the kappa opioid receptor (KOR), has been studied in the contexts of both mood and alcohol use disorders.
source: One such stress system is the neuropeptide prodynorphin (Pdyn) and its receptor, the kappa opioid receptor (KOR), which has been studied in the contexts of both mood and alcohol use disorders (Lutz and Kieffer, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lutz and Kieffer, 2013.

claim: Limbic structures implicated in alcohol and stress behaviors, such as the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), are rich in Pdyn and KOR.
source: Limbic structures implicated in alcohol and stress behaviors, such as the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), are rich in Pdyn and KOR (Le Merrer et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Le Merrer et al., 2009.

claim: The BNST is an integrative hub that may mediate the negative affective state associated with chronic alcohol use and withdrawal.
source: The BNST is an integrative hub that may mediate the negative affective state associated with chronic alcohol use and withdrawal (Koob, 2009; Kash, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koob, 2009 and Kash, 2012.

claim: KORs throughout the extended amygdala and the BNST alter anxiety-like behavior in mice.
source: KORs throughout the extended amygdala and the BNST alter anxiety-like behavior in mice (Bruchas et al., 2009; Crowley et al., 2016) and mediate stress-induced reinstatement for alcohol reinforcement (Lê et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bruchas et al., 2009 and Crowley et al., 2016.

claim: KORs mediate stress-induced reinstatement for alcohol reinforcement.
source: KORs throughout the extended amygdala and the BNST alter anxiety-like behavior in mice (Bruchas et al., 2009; Crowley et al., 2016) and mediate stress-induced reinstatement for alcohol reinforcement (Lê et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lê et al., 2018.

claim: In rats and C57BL/6J mice, TMT activates specific brain regions involved in stress, anxiety, and fear, including the BNST.
source: In rats and C57BL/6J mice, TMT activates specific brain regions involved in stress, anxiety, and fear, including the BNST (Day et al., 2004; Asok et al., 2013; Janitzky et al., 2015), and inactivation of the BNST blocks TMT-induced freezing (Fendt et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Day et al., 2004; Asok et al., 2013; and Janitzky et al., 2015.

claim: Inactivation of the BNST blocks TMT-induced freezing.
source: In rats and C57BL/6J mice, TMT activates specific brain regions involved in stress, anxiety, and fear, including the BNST (Day et al., 2004; Asok et al., 2013; Janitzky et al., 2015), and inactivation of the BNST blocks TMT-induced freezing (Fendt et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fendt et al., 2003.

claim: Distinct neuropeptide circuits in the BNST may drive opposing emotional states.
source: Recent work suggests that distinct neuropeptide circuits in the BNST may drive opposing emotional states (Giardino et al., 2018), which may be dependent on inputs from cortical sites to affect stress coping behaviors (Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Giardino et al., 2018.

claim: Distinct neuropeptide circuits in the BNST may be dependent on inputs from cortical sites to affect stress coping behaviors.
source: Recent work suggests that distinct neuropeptide circuits in the BNST may drive opposing emotional states (Giardino et al., 2018), which may be dependent on inputs from cortical sites to affect stress coping behaviors (Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2019.

claim: Dysregulation of cortical inputs to BNST Pdyn neurons and BNST Pdyn neurons themselves underlie lasting behavioral changes to stressors that emerge after chronic drinking.
source: We show that dysregulation of cortical inputs to BNST Pdyn neurons and BNST Pdyn neurons themselves underlie lasting behavioral changes to stressors that emerge after chronic drinking.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by optogenetic and genetic manipulation data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Burying in response to an immediate threat is commonly interpreted as an innate, active coping behavior in rodents.
source: Burying in response to an immediate threat is commonly interpreted as an innate, active coping behavior in rodents (De Boer and Koolhaas, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to De Boer and Koolhaas, 2003.

claim: KOR antagonists can block anxiety-like behaviors precipitated by acute withdrawal from alcohol vapor.
source: These results are in line with literature showing KOR antagonists can block anxiety-like behaviors precipitated by acute withdrawal from alcohol vapor (Valdez and Harshberger, 2012; Rose et al., 2016) and suppress alcohol self-administration in post-dependent rats (Walker and Koob, 2008; Schank et al., 2012; Kissler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Valdez and Harshberger, 2012 and Rose et al., 2016.

claim: KOR antagonists suppress alcohol self-administration in post-dependent rats.
source: These results are in line with literature showing KOR antagonists can block anxiety-like behaviors precipitated by acute withdrawal from alcohol vapor (Valdez and Harshberger, 2012; Rose et al., 2016) and suppress alcohol self-administration in post-dependent rats (Walker and Koob, 2008; Schank et al., 2012; Kissler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Walker and Koob, 2008; Schank et al., 2012; and Kissler et al., 2014.

claim: BNST norBNI attenuates stress-induced alcohol seeking.
source: KORs in the BNST appear to be particularly important in mediating interactions between stress and alcohol drinking, as BNST norBNI attenuates stress-induced alcohol seeking (Lê et al., 2018) and reduces alcohol withdrawal-induced 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalizations (Erikson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lê et al., 2018.

claim: BNST norBNI reduces alcohol withdrawal-induced 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalizations.
source: KORs in the BNST appear to be particularly important in mediating interactions between stress and alcohol drinking, as BNST norBNI attenuates stress-induced alcohol seeking (Lê et al., 2018) and reduces alcohol withdrawal-induced 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalizations (Erikson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Erikson et al., 2018.

claim: Chronic EtOH exposure and withdrawal can impact BNST spontaneous glutamatergic and NMDAR function.
source: Altogether, while other studies have found that chronic EtOH exposure and withdrawal can impact BNST spontaneous glutamatergic and NMDAR function (Kash et al., 2009; Wills et al., 2012; McElligott and Winder, 2009), our findings are the first to highlight plastic shifts in response to stressors and identify pathway-specific alterations in neuropeptide signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kash et al., 2009; Wills et al., 2012; and McElligott and Winder, 2009.

claim: Previous work found that both central amygdala (CeA) and basolateral amygdala (BLA) inputs to the BNST are KOR-sensitive, but mPFC inputs are KOR-insensitive.
source: Previous work in the lab found that both central amygdala (CeA) and basolateral amygdala (BLA) inputs to the BNST are KOR-sensitive, but mPFC inputs are KOR-insensitive (Crowley et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Crowley et al., 2016.

claim: Photostimulation of BLA inputs promotes anxiolysis in alcohol-naive mice.
source: Notably, photostimulation of BLA inputs promotes anxiolysis in alcohol-naive mice (Crowley et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Crowley et al., 2016.

claim: Prelimbic (PL) layer 2/3 neurons are a population engaged in response to acute TMT.
source: We have previously identified prelimbic (PL) layer 2/3 neurons as a population engaged in response to acute TMT using a combination of slice physiology and immunohistochemical approaches (Hwa et al., 2019), providing converging data for engagement of this pathway by this specific aversive stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hwa et al., 2019.

claim: Pdyn/KOR signaling in the CeA appears to promote EtOH consumption.
source: However, while Pdyn/KOR signaling in the CeA appears to promote EtOH consumption (Bloodgood et al., 2020), Pdyn/KOR signaling in the BNST did not affect EtOH drinking in our study.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bloodgood et al., 2020.

claim: Activation of the PL to BNST circuit negatively correlated with freezing behavior in response to a shock prod.
source: Activation of the PL to BNST circuit negatively correlated with freezing behavior, a measure of passive coping, in response to a shock prod, while photoinhibition increased freezing and decreased burying, a measure of active coping.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2019 in the discussion section.

claim: Photoinhibition of the PL to BNST circuit increased freezing and decreased burying in response to a shock prod.
source: Activation of the PL to BNST circuit negatively correlated with freezing behavior, a measure of passive coping, in response to a shock prod, while photoinhibition increased freezing and decreased burying, a measure of active coping.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnson et al., 2019 in the discussion section.

claim: Increased corticolimbic drive may promote abnormal stress behavioral responses to predator odor during protracted withdrawal.
source: These findings suggest that increased corticolimbic drive may promote abnormal stress behavioral responses to predator odor during protracted withdrawal.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic and chemogenetic data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Various nodes of the PFC-BNST dynorphin-related circuit may serve as potential targets for potential therapeutic mediation as well as biomarkers of negative responses to stress following heavy alcohol drinking.
source: Various nodes of this PFC-BNST dynorphin-related circuit may serve as potential targets for potential therapeutic mediation as well as biomarkers of negative responses to stress following heavy alcohol drinking.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and represents a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Altered mPFC-BNST connectivity could serve as a potential biomarker of negative outcomes in alcohol use disorder.
source: Further, our findings suggest that increased corticolimbic connectivity may underlie this phenomenon; thus, altered mPFC-BNST connectivity could serve as a potential biomarker of negative outcomes in alcohol use disorder.
evidence: The claim is stated in the conclusions section and represents a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Disentangling the imbalance of corticolimbic-driven stress neuropeptide signaling may lead to the development of novel therapeutics to enhance stress coping in persons with alcohol use disorder.
source: Disentangling this imbalance of corticolimbic-driven stress neuropeptide signaling may lead to the development of novel therapeutics to enhance stress coping in persons with alcohol use disorder.
evidence: The claim is stated in the conclusions section and represents a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Mitigating stress responses can contribute to improved alcohol relapse outcomes.
source: This is a critical area of study, as mitigating stress responses can contribute to improved alcohol relapse outcomes.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and represents a general inference based on established knowledge.

claim: KOR signaling in the BNST is a critical pharmacological target for treatment of alcohol use disorders.
source: Taken together, this body of evidence suggests that KOR signaling in the BNST is a critical pharmacological target for treatment of alcohol use disorders.
evidence: The claim is stated in the discussion section and represents an inference based on the experimental findings and cited literature.
